timeline.title: Born into slavery
timeline.text: Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey was born into slavery on Maryland's Eastern Shore, probably in February 1818. No record of his birth was kept, and he himself guessed 1817. Later he chose 14 February as his birthday, remembering that his mother called him her "Little Valentine". He was raised by his grandmother, Betsy Bailey.

timeline.place: Wye House, Talbot County, Maryland, (United States)
timeline.title: Taken from his grandmother
timeline.text: At about six, he was taken from his grandmother to the large Wye House plantation, where Aaron Anthony worked as overseer for the Lloyd family. He rarely saw his mother, Harriet Bailey, who lived about 12 miles away.

timeline.title: His mother dies
timeline.text: His mother died when he was about seven. He wrote that he never saw her by daylight and was not allowed to be with her when she was ill.

timeline.title: Sent to Baltimore
timeline.text: He was sent to Baltimore to serve Hugh and Sophia Auld. He later called leaving the plantation one of the most interesting events of his life. City life opened the door to learning.

timeline.title: The alphabet, then a ban
timeline.text: Sophia Auld began teaching him the alphabet. Hugh Auld stopped her, saying learning would spoil a slave. Douglass said that warning showed him the pathway from slavery to freedom. He kept learning in secret, often from white boys in the street.

timeline.title: The Columbian Orator
timeline.text: Around age 12 he spent fifty cents he had earned on The Columbian Orator, a school book of famous speeches. He read it again and again. It gave him words for his own thoughts about freedom.

timeline.place: St. Michaels, Talbot County, Maryland, (United States)
timeline.title: Sent to a slave-breaker
timeline.text: Thomas Auld took him back from Baltimore and, on 1 January 1833, hired him out for a year to Edward Covey, a farmer known for "breaking" enslaved young men with hard work and beatings.

timeline.title: He stands his ground
timeline.text: After months of abuse, Douglass resisted Covey and fought back. Covey never whipped him again. Douglass wrote that this fight was the turning-point in his career as a slave. His Narrative places it in August 1833; some sources give his age as 16, because his birth year is uncertain.

timeline.title: A secret Sabbath school
timeline.text: Hired out to William Freeland in 1834 and 1835, he quietly ran a Sunday school, teaching other enslaved people to read. At one time he had over forty students. He called it the sweetest work he had ever done.

timeline.title: An escape plan fails
timeline.text: Douglass and a few friends planned to escape by canoe up the Chesapeake Bay over the Easter holidays. They were betrayed before they left and jailed. His books disagree on the year: the Narrative suggests 1835, My Bondage and My Freedom says 1836.

timeline.title: A trade in the shipyards
timeline.text: Sent back to Baltimore, he learned to caulk ships at Fell's Point and soon earned top wages, though he had to hand them to Hugh Auld. Sources give 1835 or 1836 for this step.

timeline.title: Meets Anna Murray
timeline.text: He met Anna Murray, a free Black woman living in Baltimore. A year later she joined him in freedom.

timeline.place: Baltimore, Maryland, to New York City, (United States)
timeline.title: Escape by train
timeline.text: On 3 September 1838, dressed as a sailor and carrying borrowed seaman's papers, he boarded a northbound train. By train, ferry and steamboat he reached New York City in under a day. He hid the details for years to protect those who helped him.

timeline.place: New York City, New York, (United States)
timeline.title: Married to Anna
timeline.text: Anna Murray joined him in New York, and they married on 15 September 1838, eleven days after he arrived. They moved on to New Bedford, Massachusetts.

timeline.title: A new name, honest work
timeline.text: In New Bedford their host, Nathan Johnson, suggested the name Douglass, and he kept it for life. He worked on the wharves loading ships and sawing wood, glad that his pay was now his own.

timeline.title: First great speech
timeline.text: At an anti-slavery convention on Nantucket he was urged to speak. Nervous, he told his story, and the crowd was moved. The Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society soon hired him as a travelling lecturer.

timeline.title: The Hundred Conventions
timeline.text: He joined a six-month tour of anti-slavery meetings across the East and Midwest. In Pendleton, Indiana, a mob attacked the speakers. A Quaker family, the Hardys, cared for him, but his injured hand never fully healed.

timeline.title: The Narrative is published
timeline.text: His first autobiography came out with prefaces by William Lloyd Garrison and Wendell Phillips. It named real people and places, which proved his story but made him easier to recapture. It sold 5,000 copies in four months.

timeline.title: Two years abroad
timeline.text: Fearing capture, he sailed for Liverpool on the Cambria. For two years he lectured across Ireland, Scotland and England, drawing large crowds and making lasting friends.

timeline.title: Legally free
timeline.text: British supporters, led by Anna and Ellen Richardson of Newcastle, raised money and bought his legal freedom from Thomas Auld. The Wikipedia article on the Narrative gives the price as $710.96.

timeline.title: The North Star
timeline.text: Back in America, he moved to Rochester and launched his own anti-slavery newspaper, The North Star. Friends warned him a former slave could not run a paper. He went ahead anyway. Its motto read: "Right is of no Sex, Truth is of no Color."

timeline.title: For women's rights
timeline.text: He was the only African American at the Seneca Falls Convention on women's rights. He spoke in favour of women's right to vote, and the resolution passed.

timeline.title: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
timeline.text: Invited by the Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society, he spoke at Corinthian Hall. He asked what the Fourth of July meant to an enslaved person, and ended with hope for the country.

timeline.title: My Bondage and My Freedom
timeline.text: His second, much longer autobiography told his story again in more depth, including his years as a free man and an editor.

timeline.title: He says no to John Brown
timeline.text: He met the abolitionist John Brown near Chambersburg and refused to join his raid on Harpers Ferry. After the raid failed in October, Douglass was nearly arrested anyway. He fled to Canada and then England.

timeline.title: Men of Color, To Arms!
timeline.text: During the Civil War he urged Black men to join the Union army. He recruited for the 54th Massachusetts, and his sons Charles and Lewis were among the first to sign up.

timeline.title: Meeting Lincoln
timeline.text: Douglass met President Abraham Lincoln at the White House to press for equal treatment of Black soldiers. They met again in 1864 to talk about helping enslaved people reach freedom.

timeline.title: The bank fails
timeline.text: He became president of the Freedman's Savings Bank in March 1874, hoping to rescue it. It was already in deep trouble and closed that summer. Many Black families lost their savings.

timeline.title: Marshal and Cedar Hill
timeline.text: President Hayes made him U.S. Marshal for the District of Columbia. The same year he bought Cedar Hill, a house on about nine acres in Anacostia, for $6,700. He made it his home from 1878 until his death.

timeline.title: Recorder of Deeds and Life and Times
timeline.text: He became Recorder of Deeds for the District of Columbia and published his third autobiography, Life and Times of Frederick Douglass. Now he could tell openly how he had escaped.

timeline.title: Anna dies
timeline.text: Anna Murray Douglass, his wife of 44 years, died at Cedar Hill.

timeline.title: Marries Helen Pitts
timeline.text: He married Helen Pitts, a white suffragist 20 years younger. The marriage caused public controversy. They stayed together until his death.

timeline.title: Minister to Haiti
timeline.text: President Harrison named him U.S. Minister Resident and Consul General to Haiti. He served until 1891, and Haiti later chose him to help run its pavilion at the Chicago World's Fair.

timeline.title: His last day
timeline.text: He spent the day at a meeting of the National Council of Women, where he was welcomed with a standing ovation. That evening he died of a heart attack at Cedar Hill. He was buried in Mount Hope Cemetery in Rochester.

timeline.title: A statue in Rochester
timeline.text: A statue of Douglass was unveiled in Rochester, the city where he had printed his newspapers for many years.

timeline.title: Cedar Hill for everyone
timeline.text: After his death, Helen Pitts Douglass worked to save the house. It joined the National Park System in 1962 and became the Frederick Douglass National Historic Site in 1988. His library of more than 1,000 books is still there.

works.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
works.text: His first autobiography, short and powerful, naming real people and places to prove slavery's cruelty. It sold nearly 30,000 copies by 1860.

works.title: My Bondage and My Freedom
works.text: His second autobiography, longer and more reflective, covering his first years of freedom and his work as an editor.

works.title: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass
works.text: His third autobiography, revised in 1892. It finally told how he escaped and covered the Civil War, his meetings with Lincoln, and his public offices.

works.title: The North Star
works.text: His own anti-slavery weekly, first published in Rochester on 3 December 1847, with the motto "Right is of no Sex, Truth is of no Color".

works.title: Frederick Douglass' Paper
works.text: In 1851 The North Star merged with Gerrit Smith's Liberty Party Paper to form Frederick Douglass' Paper. During the Civil War his paper appeared as Douglass' Monthly.

works.title: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
works.text: His most famous speech, given in Rochester on 5 July 1852, asking a free nation to look honestly at slavery while still holding out hope.

works.title: The Heroic Slave
works.text: His only published work of fiction, based on Madison Washington, who led the 1841 revolt on the ship Creole that freed 135 people.

works.title: The Sabbath school
works.text: While still enslaved, he secretly taught more than forty people to read on Sundays, at great risk to them all.

works.title: Letter to Thomas Auld
works.text: An open letter to his former owner, condemning him for keeping Douglass's family enslaved and unable to read.

works.title: Speech at Seneca Falls
works.text: The only Black attendee at the first women's rights convention, he spoke up for women's right to vote.

works.title: Men of Color, To Arms!
works.text: A printed call, published on 21 March 1863, urging Black men to fight for the Union and for freedom.

works.title: Marshal, Recorder of Deeds, Minister to Haiti
works.text: He served as U.S. Marshal for the District of Columbia (1877-1881), Recorder of Deeds (1881-1886) and Minister to Haiti (1889-1891).

works.title: The Cedar Hill library
works.text: At Cedar Hill he built a library of more than 1,000 books and wrote in a small stone study he called the Growlery.
